qs.q: In bacillary angiomatosis, which Bartonella species is associated with cat-scratch disease in immunocompetent hosts and has the domestic cat as its reservoir?
qs.e: Bartonella henselae is transmitted by cats and causes cat-scratch disease. Bartonella quintana is transmitted by body lice and caused trench fever.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which Bartonella bacteria induce vascular proliferation in bacillary angiomatosis?
o: Stimulation of T-cell mediated immune response causing granuloma formation
Secretion of viral cyclin D homologues that inhibit p53
Induction of host tissue production of HIF-1α, which drives VEGF production
Direct destruction of endothelial cells leading to compensatory hyperplasia
qs.e: Bartonella induces HIF-1α production in host tissues, which drives VEGF production and subsequent vascular proliferation. Viral cyclin D is associated with HHV8/KS.

exam: What bedside clues would make you suspect bacillary angiomatosis over Kaposi sarcoma? — Bright red, friable lesions, HIV status, and positive Warthin‑Starry stain.
A patient with AIDS presents with multiple liver nodules; how do you confirm the diagnosis? — Perform liver biopsy with silver stain or PCR for Bartonella.
Why is doxycycline preferred as first‑line therapy? — It is bacteriostatic, intracellularly active, and has a favorable safety profile in HIV patients.
If doxycycline is contraindicated, what alternative regimen would you choose and why? — Erythromycin, because it also targets Bartonella but requires careful hepatic monitoring.

How would you differentiate a bacillary angiomatosis lesion from a pyogenic granuloma clinically? — BA lesions are multiple, bright red, and occur in immunocompromised hosts; pyogenic granuloma is solitary, follows trauma, and shows neutrophilic inflammation.

What are the urgent complications of visceral bacillary angiomatosis you must monitor for? — Hepatic or splenic rupture, bone fracture, CNS hemorrhage; these require immediate surgical or neuro‑critical care.

In a low‑resource setting without PCR, how do you proceed when the silver stain is negative but suspicion remains high? — Treat empirically with doxycycline while arranging follow‑up for clinical response.
What preventive measures reduce the risk of bacillary angiomatosis in HIV patients? — Effective antiretroviral therapy, cat‑avoidance or flea control, and lice control in crowded living conditions.
ai.title: Bacillary Angiomatosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A vascular proliferative lesion caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV/AIDS. Presents with bright red papules or nodules that can involve skin, liver, spleen, and bone. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and special stains, with treatment directed at the bacteria.

b: Endothelial proliferation driven by HIF‑1α and VEGF
Warthin‑Starry silver stain or PCR shows bacilli
sections.p: Bacillary angiomatosis is a benign, rapidly growing vascular lesion caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana infection in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

t.b: Confirms presence of bacilli; positive stain supports BA versus Kaposi sarcoma
Detects species; useful when stain unavailable
Shows endothelial nature; helps differentiate from inflammatory lesions

b: Mild: isolated skin lesions
Moderate: skin + one visceral organ (liver, spleen, bone)
Severe: multiple organ involvement, systemic fever, anemia
sections.p: Severity is gauged by organ involvement and systemic symptoms rather than a formal stage system.

b: Bartonella henselae – cat scratches/bites, common in East Africa where stray cats are prevalent
Bartonella quintana – body louse transmission, linked to crowded living conditions and homelessness
sections.p: Opportunistic Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts.

b: Lesions often bleed easily on minor trauma
Systemic signs: low‑grade fever, weight loss, night sweats
Visceral disease: hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, neurologic deficits if CNS involved
sections.p: Patients present with painless, bright red to violaceous papules or nodules that may ulcerate; lesions can be solitary or widespread.
Targeted tests confirm Bartonella infection and assess organ involvement.

t.b: Detect anemia or leukopenia; anemia may reflect chronic disease or bone involvement
Identify hepatic or splenic nodules when imaging is available
Detect CNS lesions; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and CSF analysis

b: Massive hepatic or splenic lesions → rupture, hemorrhage
Bone involvement → pathological fracture
CNS lesions → seizures or focal deficits
sections.p: Complications arise from extensive visceral disease or secondary infection.

b: Avoid macrolide monotherapy in severe disease without doxycycline due to slower response
sections.p: Treat the underlying Bartonella infection and provide supportive care.

b: Re‑examine skin lesions every 2 weeks; expect gradual fading
Repeat imaging if visceral lesions were present
Encourage ART adherence in HIV, improve hygiene to reduce lice exposure
sections.p: Monitor lesion regression and immune status; educate on vector avoidance.

b: Kaposi sarcoma – HHV‑8 positive, spindle cells, often in AIDS; lesions are darker, less exophytic, and Warthin‑Starry stain negative
Pyogenic granuloma – rapid growth after trauma, neutrophilic inflammation, no bacilli on stain
